# Delivery

Every Skill that produces a Text Artifact delivers it the same way. This document is the complete contract: where a result goes, how a response carries the text, what the response carries when it went somewhere else, when a source file may be replaced instead, what happens when nothing changed, what language a run's own words about the text are written in and whether what those words say is true of the text they name, and what is refused before anything is written. It is a reference several Skills read rather than a runtime of its own. Each Skill exposes these rules through its own Formal Invocation and owns the names it gives them, so nothing here fixes how an option is spelled; what is fixed is the behaviour behind it.

## The response is the default

The default Output Target is the agent response. A run that keeps the default delivers the complete Text Artifact in the response and changes nothing on the filesystem: it creates no file, touches no file, and makes no directory. That includes scratch files and working copies of the artifact, wherever the Harness says temporary files belong.

A Harness convention identifies where an authorized temporary file belongs; it does not authorize a write. If a run genuinely needs a scratch file while composing, it removes that file before delivery and restores the filesystem to the state in which it found it. Before reporting delivery, the run checks the filesystem locations it used, including the Harness scratch area, and never reports that nothing was written while a copy of the artifact remains on disk.

An Output Target is independent of where the source material came from. Supplying a local file as source material selects no destination, and a run that reads a file still delivers to the response until the caller names somewhere else. Persisting a result is the caller's explicit choice, and making that choice is the whole of the authorization for it.

## How a response carries the text

A response carries a Text Artifact inside a fenced code block rather than as prose of the reply's own. A text and the words about it are two different things, and a reply that runs them together hands the reader a text nothing marks the edges of. Markdown is where that costs most: an artifact opening on a frontmatter delimiter, set directly beneath a paragraph the run wrote, turns that paragraph into a heading unless a blank line goes in between them — and a blank line there is what ends the frontmatter block the text was settled with. A fence removes the question rather than leaving each run to answer it, and the answers a run improvises are what made one saved reply in sixteen deliver a horizontal rule and a paragraph of configuration in place of a frontmatter block.

The complete Text Artifact sits inside exactly one fenced code block, byte for byte as the run settled it: frontmatter, blank lines and trailing structure included. Nothing is added, dropped or re-wrapped between the fence lines, and one block rather than several, a text split across two fences being a text the reader has to reassemble.

The fence is longer than the longest run of backticks inside the artifact, so a text carrying fenced code of its own cannot close it early. The info string names the text's format: `markdown` for a Markdown text, `html` for HTML, `text` for plain text.

Everything the run says *about* the text sits outside the fence — the resolved configuration, the findings and which of them are unresolved, the claim account, where a technique came from, what the run could not do. Nothing of the run's own is inside it. What the run settled as part of the document does belong inside, the Handoff Metadata and any marking the user asked to have placed in the document itself among it, because that is the text as delivered rather than a remark about it.

The rule reaches every complete text a reply carries, whether this contract calls that text delivered or not. A response-targeted run that changed nothing and has findings left fences the artifact like any other; a run that stopped before it could deliver and carries its preserved prose in the reply fences that prose, and says in its own words outside the fence what the prose has not been through. The short no-change status carries no text at all and so carries no fence. An explicit destination and In-place Editing receive the text itself and never a fence: a fence is how a reply holds a text apart from its own words, and a file has no words of its own to be held apart from.

## An explicit destination

An explicit destination is one filesystem path, and what exists at that path decides what happens to it.

**A path that does not exist** creates exactly that one file and writes the complete Text Artifact into it. Exactly one file: nothing else is created beside it, and no directory is made to hold it.

**A path naming an existing file** overwrites that exact file with the complete Text Artifact. No confirmation and no separate force option is required, and none is offered. Naming the path is the authorization, and demanding a second gesture on top of it would teach that naming a destination means something less than it says.

**A path naming an existing directory** delivers into that directory under a filename the run derives, by the rules below. Choosing a directory selects a place, not a file, so it never overwrites a file already in it.

## Deriving a filename for a directory

A directory destination needs a name, and the name comes from what the run already knows. Take the first of these the run has: the basename of the local file that supplied the Text Artifact, the title of a referenced URL, then the Skill's own working title for the text it created. Reduce it to a name the filesystem accepts, and keep a suitable text extension — the source file's own where it had one, and otherwise the one matching the text's format.

That gives a stem and an extension, and the stem stays as it is for every delivery into that directory. Where nothing exists at the derived name, that name is the file written. Where something exists there, the existing file is never overwritten: keep the original stem and take the first free numbered candidate in ascending order, beginning at `-2`. So `my-file.md`, `my-file-2.md`, `my-file-3.md` are one sequence, growing by one name at a time.

A numbered candidate is never adopted as the new stem. A third delivery into a directory already holding the first two is `my-file-3.md` and never `my-file-2-2.md`, whose stem would fork the sequence in two and leave the directory recording how many times the same text arrived rather than which arrival it was. Ascending order with the first free name also means a number freed by a deleted file is used again before a higher one is taken.

## What the response carries when a destination was named

A run that delivers to an explicit destination does not repeat the Text Artifact in the response. The response says where the text went — the derived filename included, where the destination was a directory — and carries what the file cannot: the findings the run reports beside the text, and which of them are unresolved. Naming a destination is saying where the text goes, and printing it again spends output on what the caller is already holding, doubly so when the file just written holds it too.

That holds whether or not the pass changed anything. A run that writes a file byte-identical to the source it read reports the destination and says the text needed no work, and does not become the one run that echoes a text the caller had before it started. The response is the default target precisely because a run that names no destination has nowhere else to put the artifact; naming one moves the text out of the response rather than duplicating it there.

## In-place Editing

In-place Editing replaces the single local file that supplied the Text Artifact with the result, instead of delivering it anywhere else. It is available only to a Skill whose work is to return a changed version of a text the caller already has.

A Skill that creates a new Text Artifact

**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.

**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.

**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.

**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.

**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. Stacked short fragments used for drama — *That's it. That's the whole idea.* — are the same fault at the other extreme. Read a passage aloud in your head; where the breath falls in the same place every time, the shape is doing the writing. Vary length and construction where the meaning gives you a reason to, and merge or split only the sentences whose shape is actually the problem.

**Generic conclusions.** A final paragraph that restates what the reader has just read, reopens the introduction as a rhetorical question, or reaches for an uplifting abstraction: *In conclusion*, *Ultimately, the future belongs to those who…*, *one thing is clear.* The reader was there for the whole text and does not need it summarised back. Delete the paragraph and end on the last concrete point the draft already contains; where the job genuinely calls for a conclusion, a recommendation, or a next step, write that thing plainly and stop. 1	# Delivery

3	Every Skill that produces a Text Artifact delivers it the same way. It is a reference several Skills read rather than a runtime of its own. Each Skill exposes these rules through its own Formal Invocation and owns the names it gives them, so nothing here fixes how an option is spelled; what is fixed is the behaviour behind it.
4	
5	## The response is the default
6	
7	The default Output Target is the agent response. A run that keeps the default delivers the complete Text Artifact in the response and changes nothing on the filesystem: it creates no file, touches no file, and makes no directory. That includes scratch files and working copies of the artifact, wherever the Harness says temporary files belong.
8	
9	A Harness convention identifies where an authorized temporary file belongs; it does not authorize a write. If a run genuinely needs a scratch file while composing, it removes that file before delivery and restores the filesystem to the state in which it found it. Before reporting delivery, the run checks the filesystem locations it used, including the Harness scratch area, and never reports that nothing was written while a copy of the artifact remains on disk.
10	
11	An Output Target is independent of where the source material came from. Supplying a local file as source material selects no destination, and a run that reads a file still delivers to the response until the caller names somewhere else. Persisting a result is the caller's explicit choice, and making that choice is the whole of the authorization for it.
12	
13	## How a response carries the text
14	
15	A response carries a Text Artifact inside a fenced code block rather than as prose of the reply's own. A text and the words about it are two different things, and a reply that runs them together hands the reader a text nothing marks the edges of. Markdown is where that costs most: an artifact opening on a frontmatter delimiter, set directly beneath a paragraph the run wrote, turns that paragraph into a heading unless a blank line goes in between them — and a blank line there is what ends the frontmatter block the text was settled with. A fence removes the question rather than leaving each run to answer it, and the answers a run improvises are what made one saved reply in sixteen deliver a horizontal rule and a paragraph of configuration in place of a frontmatter block.
16	
17	The complete Text Artifact sits inside exactly one fenced code block, byte for byte as the run settled it: frontmatter, blank lines and trailing structure included. Nothing is added, dropped or re-wrapped between the fence lines, and one block rather than several, a text split across two fences being a text the reader has to reassemble.
18	
19	The fence is longer than the longest run of backticks inside the artifact, so a text carrying fenced code of its own cannot close it early. The info string names the text's format: `markdown` for a Markdown text, `html` for HTML, `text` for plain text.
20	
21	Everything the run says *about* the text sits outside the fence — the resolved configuration, the findings and which of them are unresolved, the claim account, where a technique came from, what the run could not do. Nothing of the run's own is inside it. What the run settled as part of the document does belong inside, the Handoff Metadata and any marking the user asked to have placed in the document itself among it, because that is the text as delivered rather than a remark about it.
22	
23	The rule reaches every complete text a reply carries, whether this contract calls that text delivered or not. The short no-change status carries no text at all and so carries no fence. An explicit destination and In-place Editing receive the text itself and never a fence: a fence is how a reply holds a text apart from its own words, and a file has no words of its own to be held apart from.
24	
25	## An explicit destination
26	
27	An explicit destination is one filesystem path, and what exists at that path decides what happens to it.
28	
29	**A path that does not exist** creates exactly that one file and writes the complete Text Artifact into it. Exactly one file: nothing else is created beside it, and no directory is made to hold it.
30	
31	**A path naming an existing file** overwrites that exact file with the complete Text Artifact. No confirmation and no separate force option is required, and none is offered. Naming the path is the authorization, and demanding a second gesture on top of it would teach that naming a destination means something less than it says.
32	
33	**A path naming an existing directory** delivers into that directory under a filename the run derives, by the rules below. Choosing a directory selects a place, not a file, so it never overwrites a file already in it.
34	
35	## Deriving a filename for a directory
36	
37	A directory destination needs a name, and the name comes from what the run already knows. Take the first of these the run has: the basename of the local file that supplied the Text Artifact, the title of a referenced URL, then the Skill's own working title for the text it created. 38	
39	That gives a stem and an extension, and the stem stays as it is for every delivery into that directory. Where nothing exists at the derived name, that name is the file written. 40	
41	A numbered candidate is never adopted as the new stem. 42	
43	## What the response carries when a destination was named
44	
45	A run that delivers to an explicit destination does not repeat the Text Artifact in the response. 46	
47	That holds whether or not the pass changed anything. 48	
49	## In-place Editing
50	
51	In-place Editing replaces the single local file that supplied the Text Artifact with the result, instead of delivering it anywhere else. It is available only to a Skill whose work is to return a changed version of a text the caller already has.
52	
53	A Skill that creates a new Text Artifact never edits its own source material in place. 58

62	
63	A run may finish with nothing to change, and what it does then follows its destination.
64	
65	A response-targeted run that changed nothing returns a short no-change status in place of the text when no unresolved findings remain. When findings remain, deliver the complete Text Artifact in the response and report the unresolved findings separately.

68

70	
71	An explicitly selected different file or directory still receives the complete Text Artifact when nothing changed. 72	
73	## The language of a report about the text
74	
75	A run that reports on the text beside the text itself — the findings it carries forward, and which of them are unresolved — writes that report in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, exactly as the no-change status above is written. 76	
77	Who reads it is what decides this. A report about a text is read by the reader of that text, who has to finish whatever the run left undone, and a report in whichever language the invocation happened to be written in reaches that reader in a language nothing about the text promised. The invocation's language is how the run was asked for; the artifact's language is what the run is about.
78	
79	## The truth of a report about the text
80	
81	Everything a run says about a text is true of the text it names. That holds for every statement the reply makes about a text, and not only for its findings and its account of the claims: a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, and what a round did to a passage — moved it, removed it, replaced it, set a heading over it — each tells the reader something about the text they could check, and each is written so that the check holds.
82	
83	A statement about the delivered text is checked against the delivered text after the last change to it, the closing mechanical pass included. 84	
85	The check is made on the reply as drafted, one statement at a time, once the text it describes is final, and each statement is read against the passage it names rather than against what the run remembers of it; a finding written during the review is checked in the same way against the text it was written about. 86	
87	Who reads it decides this too. The reader of a report finds their way in the text by it, and a statement they check and find false costs them the trust they would have given every other statement in the same reply.
88

90	
91	Every contradictory, meaningless, or unusable output request is refused before the first side effect. 92

94	
95	A refusal follows the Collection's ordinary diagnostic and help conventions. An output option is refused rather than ignored where it has no work to do, a flag accepted and ignored teaching that flags sometimes do nothing.

You are making one correction to one text. You have not seen this text before, and there is nothing you are expected to remember: the text below is its current state, and the findings below are the current review's, complete and as they were written. Repair them.

**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

````markdown
# Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came down from the shelf. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

The usual advice is a weekly habit: photograph each receipt, match the week's photographs to your bank lines every Friday, and note anything odd. It is good advice, and it asks for fifty-two Fridays a year from people who already work most of them.

There is another way to get the weekend back. In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who matched receipts every week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who left everything until January reported 19. But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference. Still, the shortest January in the survey belonged to the people who did the least bookkeeping themselves.

A tutor's time is worth more at the whiteboard than at the kitchen table sorting paper. The tin does not have to become a Friday chore. It can become somebody else's job.

This January, the tin could leave the house before the last weekend does.
````

(The fence is not part of the text. The text ends with one newline after "does.")

So a finding you cannot repair without creating another one is a finding you leave and say so, exactly as you would one you cannot repair without inventing a fact — an unrepaired finding a person can settle costs less than a repair that has to be thrown away with everything beside it.

**What a repair may take with it, and what it may not.** A finding names a defect, and what a repair removes is that defect. Where the defect a finding names is the whole of the passage — an opening that would sit in front of any text, a closing that restates what the reader has just read, a claim credited to nobody that the text cannot source — removing it may be the repair, and any claim removed with it must be named in your return. That stops at a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts — that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that the text is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Remove or weaken one only where the finding names a defect inside the sentence, and only where a sentence you keep still states that limit in full, so the text bounds what it claims exactly as far as it did, or where the limit contradicts another passage of the same text. Otherwise leave it exactly as it stands and say so. Where the passage carries a claim beside the defect — a fact, an observation, the point the passage exists to make — the smallest change is the one that leaves that claim standing, and deleting the passage entire is not that change. And where you can see no way to remove the defect that does not take the claim with it, leave the passage alone and say so, exactly as you would a finding you cannot repair without inventing a fact: a person can give that claim what it needs or let it go, and a round that deletes it leaves them nothing to weigh. That judgement is about the passage in front of you and never about how much of the text is left — a short text is no licence to leave a finding standing, and a long one is no licence to go on cutting.

A repair at a punctuation joint can be the smallest change even when the finding names the implication created there rather than punctuation itself. In *We finished in March, the finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*, the defect is the implication created by joining unrelated claims, not either claim. Repair it as *We finished in March. The finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*: splitting at the joint removes the implication and keeps the reporting-tool fact. Do the same wherever the named defect is confined to a joint; do not delete either side or supply a relationship the text does not establish. This example does not admit a wider mechanics pass: it identifies the smallest repair for the finding already in hand.

Before you return the text, compare it before and after, claim by claim. Every claim you received must still appear with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality and meaning intact unless the finding named the whole claim as the defect; that exception does not reach a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts, which goes only on the two conditions above, and the number or concentration of findings changes nothing about that check. The concentrated anti-slop case makes the boundary visible: removing its patterns must not discard its claims about meeting load, documentation, decisions, satisfaction, distributed work, adoption conditions, or the synchronous/asynchronous trade-off. Repair the patterns around those claims. If one cannot be separated from its pattern, keep it and report the finding unresolved; never compress several content-bearing passages into a cleaner summary.

**Your own working files.** Any file you write for your own working purposes — a candidate you measure, a draft you compare, anything you keep while you work — goes in a directory you created for this one round, under a name made unique when you created it, such as the one `mktemp -d` returns. Remove that directory before you return, including on failure. A fixed name under a shared temporary directory is not that directory, whether the directory is the system's own or a scratchpad your session was given: another run may be working at the same time, in the same place and on this same text, and write that same name. The file you come back to is then that run's work and not yours, and when you take it for your own stale copy and delete or replace it, you destroy work that is not yours, and nothing tells the run it came from.

**What you return.** The complete corrected text and a short note of which findings you repaired and which you left, with the reason for each you left. Where any repair removed a passage carrying a claim, name every removed claim and say which finding made the claim itself the defect, and name every changed claim the same way — one you left standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved, by what it now asserts rather than how far its wording moved, and the finding the repair that moved it answered. Where a repair took a limit, a connective or a bounding clause out of the text — a sentence or a heading saying what is not measured, not claimed or not known, a connective giving the text's own reason for what follows, a clause saying what a claim is not about — say what a reader of the text you return no longer has, however little of the text went with it. Name every added claim the same way, whether or not anything was removed: one the text you return asserts and the text you received has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say, and the finding the repair that wrote it answered. A claim with a counterpart in the text you received is changed rather than added. Reporting a removal never makes an impermissible one acceptable. The complete text: not a diff, not the changed passages, not a description of what you did. Return no commentary inside the text itself.

I repaired Findings 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6. I left Findings 5 and 7 as the review instructed. No working files were written.

````markdown
# Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came out. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

In March 2026, Priya moved to a session every Friday: "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea." She photographs each receipt when she gets it, and on Friday she matches the week's photographs to her bank lines and notes anything odd.

In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who said they matched receipts at least once a week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who said they left receipts until January reported 19. But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference.

Priya's habit also answers the tin's quieter cost. As our support team notes, a photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable.
````

**Repaired**
- **Finding 4:** "came down from the shelf" is now "came out". The claim that the tin came out every January is unchanged.
- **Finding 2:** "The usual advice" is gone. The steps are now credited to Priya, in the words of material.md §2. One claim changed: she photographs each receipt "when she gets it", not just "each receipt".
- **Findings 1 and 3:** I removed every claim Finding 1 names whole as the defect:
  - the habit asks for fifty-two Fridays from people who already work most of them, including "It is good advice" in the same sentence;
  - there is another way to get the weekend back;
  - the shortest January belonged to those who did the least bookkeeping themselves;
  - a tutor's time is worth more at the whiteboard than at the kitchen table;
  - the tin does not have to become a Friday chore;
  - the tin can become somebody else's job;
  - this January the tin could leave the house before the last weekend does.

  Two connecting words went with those sentences. "Still" set the conclusion against the survey's own limit. "There is another way" introduced the survey as a remedy. Removing paragraph 6 also removed the text's only "This January" timing line, which was already weak on why now (see Finding 7).
- **Finding 6:** the survey groups now say "said they matched receipts at least once a week" and "said they left receipts until January".

**Kept on purpose**
- The survey sentence, its three medians and the accountant sentence are unchanged. That includes "But … just 3 hours": Finding 1 puts that sentence outside the defect, so I didn't touch it even though it still leans slightly towards accountants.
- The limit sentence "The figures are what people told us…" is unchanged and in full.

**Added claims** (all for Finding 1)
- Priya moved to a Friday session in March 2026, quoted as "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea." (material.md §2).
- A photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable, credited to the support team (material.md §3).
- A new link I drew myself: Priya's habit answers the tin's quieter cost. This rests on two things: she photographs receipts when she gets them, and the support team says such photographs stay readable.

Nothing says the habit causes a short return, that her tin is empty, or that any January will be short. The text doesn't use "January this year was an evening." It doesn't state the scanner message or mention the app, tax rules, prices or other apps.

**Left unrepaired**
- **Finding 5:** "most of us spend the months before it…" is unchanged. The material has no figure for that share, and the review said to leave it.
- **Finding 7:** why now is still missing, and paragraph 6's removal took away the only "This January" line. The early-October send-out date is in the brief, not the material, so this is for the writer.
- **Ending:** the brief wants to end on "the tin … which this January is empty". The material can't support that, so the text ends on the fading-receipt answer instead. A true return to the tin needs material showing what happened after the switch.

---
name: proofread
description: Correct only mechanical language errors — spelling, grammar, punctuation, agreement, inflection, duplicated or missing words, and locale mechanics — in one supplied text, preserving its wording, meaning, tone, structure, formatting, and metadata. Start it on your own only when a specific text is at hand and the request either uses a proofreading term (proofread, spell-check, copyedit, fix the typos, korrekturläs, rätta stavfelen) or is unambiguously limited to mechanical language errors. Not for a request to edit, rewrite, polish, improve, tighten, or review a text — each of those asks for changes this Skill refuses to make. A user may also invoke it by name at any time.
disable-model-invocation: false
argument-hint: '[--language=<language>] ([--output=response|<path>] [<text>|<path>|<url>] | --in-place[=on|off] <path>) [-- <instruction>]'
compatibility: Requires uv
metadata:

---

# proofread

Correct the mechanical language errors in one supplied Text Artifact, and change nothing else about it.

Run `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1 uv run "$HERE/scripts/invoke.py"` — `$HERE` is the directory that holds this SKILL.md — with everything the user typed after `/proofread`, verbatim and however many lines, on stdin. Exit 0: do what it prints. On any other exit, if you introduced a known construction error and can correct it while preserving the user's request and authority, account for effects already produced, submit the corrected invocation through the same shim, and continue from the failed boundary; a refusal before the operation starts consumes no operation. Otherwise show what it printed to the user verbatim and stop. Never repair input the user supplied, or automatically retry exact help, an unmet dependency, an unrelated failure, or a failure whose origin or valid correction is unknown.

Run every UV command in this Skill with a fresh private directory as `TMPDIR`, and remove that directory after the command, including when it fails. The private directory belongs to that one command and no other run, so cleanup removes only files this run created.

A model-invoked run changes only how the Skill starts. Once started, it takes the specific Text Artifact the current turn identifies as the omitted operand and enters the same numbered steps as invocation by name. The paths join before loading any language or editorial resource; the trigger wording is not a second source of rules or an alternate execution path.

Where no Formal Invocation carries an Output Target, settle it from the current turn before correcting or writing. An unnamed destination resolves to the response, and a file mentioned only as the location of the errors names no destination: the verbs *fix* and *correct* apply to the named errors, not to the file containing them. Thus `Fix the spelling and grammar mistakes in case.md` delivers to the response. A turn that explicitly names the response or a path other than the source as the destination selects that Output Target; for example, `Write the corrected text to corrected.md` selects corrected.md as a separate Output Target. A turn that asks for the file itself to be changed selects In-place Editing only when it explicitly names that file as the object of the change or as the destination of the corrected text; for example, `Update case.md with the grammar corrections` selects In-place Editing. It remains subject to every refusal that editing mode already carries, including inline text, a URL, an uploaded or read-only source, more than one text, and a simultaneous separate Output Target. A request to save, apply, or persist the corrections without naming where they go is materially ambiguous about the destination: `Fix the grammar errors in case.md and save the corrections` asks which destination the caller intends and writes nothing. For that case and any other material ambiguity about the destination, ask which destination the caller intends and write nothing.

## Arguments

The operand is the Text Artifact: inline text, one local path, or one URL, and exactly one of them — several paths, a glob reaching more than one file, or a directory of texts is more than one. Where the invocation carries no operand, it is the single text the current turn identifies.

`--output=response|<path>` names the Output Target. `response` is the default and the value `response` states it explicitly; anything else is one filesystem path. It and In-place Editing name two destinations for one text, which is why no form carries both.

`--in-place[=<value>]` selects In-place Editing. It accepts `yes`, `on`, and `true` against `no`, `off`, and `false`; bare `--in-place` means `on`, `--in-place=off` has the same effect as omitting the option, and the default is `off`.

## Steps

1. Settle the single Text Artifact and the options from the JSON. A value outside what `## Arguments` admits — `--in-place` outside its vocabulary, or more than one Text Artifact — is refused as `$LIBRARY/references/invocation-envelope.md` says: correct nothing, write nothing, and stop. Done when one Text Artifact and a valid set of options are in hand, or you have stopped.
2. Settle the destination before anything is corrected, following `$LIBRARY/references/delivery.md`. Make every refusal that contract names by reading alone — In-place Editing together with a separate Output Target, an output path equal to the input path, In-place Editing against inline text or a URL or a source that is not a writable local file, and a destination whose parent directory does not exist — so that a refusal has nothing written behind it. Done when the destination is settled, or you have stopped.
3. Read the Text Artifact's leading YAML frontmatter where it has any, and look in it for one top-level `kntnt` map. That map is the only Kntnt configuration a document carries; `language`, `lang`, `genre`, `technique`, and every other key outside it are the document's own fields, whatever they are named and whatever they hold. Read `language` out of the map and nothing else out of it. The map is never required: a Text Artifact carrying none is proofread exactly like one that carries a complete one, its absence refusing nothing and leaving the language to the levels below it in step 4. Done when the artifact's recognized language value is known to be present, absent, or unreachable.
4. Resolve the language, taking the first of these that answers: the `--language` value; the recognized `kntnt` map's `language` value from step 3; the current Contextual Instruction; applicable Conversation Context; then the language of the Text Artifact itself, which is what inference reads and what the default already is. Suppression is that precedence working rather than an error: a Contextual Instruction every higher level has already settled leaves nothing for it to settle, and the run continues rather than refusing it as unaddressable guidance. Where saying so is useful, the delivery names the suppressed instruction beside the resolved configuration. Where that language is materially ambiguous or mixed — no dominant language, or alternation inside paragraphs — ask which language to proofread in rather than choosing one. Nothing has been written yet, so asking costs nothing to undo. Done when exactly one selector is in hand, or you have asked.
5. If step 3 found a recognized `kntnt` map whose `language` value no installed resource answers to, and `--language` supplied no value, report it as unusable artifact metadata: name the value, say that it is neither a canonical code nor an installed alias, and stop. Do not read it as the code it resembles. A `--language` value settles the parameter and suppresses this, the unusable map then being none of the run's business. Done when the run has stopped, or the metadata is not in the way.

That one document is the whole of what is admitted from the Collection's editorial resources: load no base contract, no genre, no technique, and no anti-slop catalogue, load no other scope, and read no composition, review, or anti-slop guidance from anywhere. Done when the contract and the mechanics scope are both in hand, or you have stopped.
7. Correct all of them — a mechanical pass that leaves mechanical errors behind is a pass the user has to make again. Before this step is done, make an agreement-only re-read of every ordinary-prose sentence after the other corrections. Check agreement in both directions between subject and verb and between noun and modifier; in Swedish, `olika bild` must become `olika bilder`. Make that same re-read whether `--language` named the language or another level of the precedence settled it. A resolved locale establishes its date conventions but not what ambiguous source fields meant: `3/4` stays exactly `3/4` under both `en_GB` and `en_US` unless the Text Artifact itself establishes one reading; never expand or reorder it solely from locale. A grammatically valid word-as-word phrase such as `the word probably` remains unmarked: add no quotation marks or other emphasis unless the loaded rules identify an objective error. A code sample — a fenced block, an indented block, or an inline code span — is quoted material rather than the text's own prose: its contents are read past rather than read against the rules, so nothing inside one is a finding and nothing inside one is changed, the docstrings, comments, and string literals among them. Prose about code is ordinary prose and is read like every other sentence. Introduce no spellchecker, grammar service, or scanner of your own; the resolver above is the only script this Skill runs. Done when the mechanical errors you can identify are corrected.
8. Change nothing else. Wording, meaning, tone, register, argument, structure, factual content, formatting and markup, code and its contents, links, and metadata all come through untouched, and the frontmatter comes through byte for byte — a language value you were entitled to read is read and left exactly where it is, no `kntnt` map is added or removed, and nothing is reordered. A preference is not an error, and the rules step 6 put in hand are what says which is which: what neither of them names as an error comes through untouched, however tempting it is, and what either of them does name is corrected however deliberate it looks. A sentence improved here is the failure this Skill exists to prevent: mechanical correction was requested, and mechanical correction is the whole of what is delivered. Done when the diff you are about to deliver is mechanical throughout.
9. Deliver by `$LIBRARY/references/delivery.md`: the complete Text Artifact to the settled Output Target, the source file replaced where In-place Editing was requested, and a derived filename with its collisions resolved where the target is a directory. On a response target, remove every artifact or scratch file this run created and base the delivery account on the filesystem state that remains after cleanup. Where nothing was corrected and the destination is the response or the source file itself, write nothing at all and return only the short no-change status, in the language of the Text Artifact. Done when the Text Artifact has been delivered, or the no-change status has been reported.

# The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

## Lists

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.

# Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came out. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

In March 2026, Priya moved to a session every Friday: "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea." She photographs each receipt when she gets it, and on Friday she matches the week's photographs to her bank lines and notes anything odd.

In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who said they matched receipts at least once a week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who said they left receipts until January reported 19. But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference.

Priya's habit also answers the tin's quieter cost. As our support team notes, a photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable.

**Settings used:** Brief `brief.md` (from `--brief`; no other brief was named). Genre `general`, technique ABT and language `en_GB` all come from the `kntnt` map in `brief.md`. ABT was set by the brief's map, not by the genre, since `general` names no technique. `input.md` has no `kntnt` map, so the two couldn't conflict, and no map was added to it.

**What happened:** One correction round, which used the whole budget of 1, passed re-review and was kept. The review stopped there because the budget was spent. Every finding still open needs material or a decision from the writer. The final proofread found no mechanical errors and changed nothing. No files were written, and every temporary file has been removed.

````markdown
# Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came out. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

In March 2026, Priya moved to a session every Friday: "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea." She photographs each receipt when she gets it, and on Friday she matches the week's photographs to her bank lines and notes anything odd.

In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who said they matched receipts at least once a week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who said they left receipts until January reported 19. But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference.

Priya's habit also answers the tin's quieter cost. As our support team notes, a photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable.
````

## Findings

**Fixed**

1. **The text steered readers away from the weekly habit** (brief questions 3, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 2; the ABT "therefore"). Old paragraphs 3–6 called the weekly habit a burden of "fifty-two Fridays a year". They ended by handing the tin to "somebody else", meaning an accountant. That is the opposite of the brief's message, angle, conclusion and intended effect. It is also outside the brand's remit, which is bookkeeping habits and its own app. The ending also left the faded-receipt cost unanswered. Fix: those claims are gone. The "therefore" now walks through Priya's Friday session and ends on the faded receipts.
2. **Unnamed source.** "The usual advice is a weekly habit" credited the steps to nobody. They are now credited to Priya, as `material.md` gives them.
3. **A correlation offered as a solution.** Two sentences offered the accountant figure as a way out: "There is another way to get the weekend back" and "Still, the shortest January … belonged to the people who did the least bookkeeping themselves". The text's own next sentence says the figures show no cause. "Did the least bookkeeping" is also not in the material. Both sentences are gone.
4. **Invented detail.** Nothing in the material says the tin was kept "on the shelf". It now just "came out".
5. **Survey groups didn't match the source.** "Every week" and "everything" now read "said they matched receipts at least once a week" and "said they left receipts until January", as the survey puts it.

**Still open, for the writer**

6. **"most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did"** (paragraph 1). The material gives no share of sole traders who wait until January, so a figure is needed. "Us" also puts Larkspur Ledger among the sole traders, while paragraph 4 says "our users".
7. **Nothing says why now** (brief question 4). Nothing tells the reader it is early October with time left before January. Removing the old last line ("This January, …") took away the only mention of the coming January, so this is weaker than it was. The send-out date is in the brief, not in the material.
8. **The accountant figure still points the other way.** "But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours" was kept. It is a sourced claim and was not itself the problem. It is still the lowest figure, it opens with "But", and nothing after it answers it. A reader can still conclude that an accountant is the answer.
9. **"Priya's habit also answers the tin's quieter cost."** The word "also" implies that the habit fixes the lost weekend too. Nothing supports that:
   - The survey says it doesn't show cause.
   - The material has no return Priya filed after she switched.
   - The quote "January this year was an evening." can't be used. The interview is dated September 2026 and the switch March 2026, so "January this year" came before the switch.

   Material on her first return after the switch would settle it.
10. **The ending.** The brief wants to end on the tin, empty this January, but the material doesn't support that. The current ending ties back only to the faded-receipt half of the hook.

## Claim account

**Removed** (all in the one correction round)

- The tin came down "from the shelf" (finding 4 named the detail itself as the problem).
- The weekly habit is "the usual advice" (finding 2).
- "It is good advice": the text's praise for that advice went with the sentence finding 1 named. The text no longer calls the habit good advice in words. It shows Priya's habit instead.
- The habit "asks for fifty-two Fridays a year from people who already work most of them" (finding 1).
- "There is another way to get the weekend back" (findings 1 and 3). This line introduced the survey as a solution. The reader no longer sees the survey framed that way.
- "Still, the shortest January in the survey belonged to the people who did the least bookkeeping themselves" (findings 1 and 3). "Still" set this against the survey's caveat. The caveat stays in full.
- "A tutor's time is worth more at the whiteboard than at the kitchen table sorting paper" (finding 1).
- "The tin does not have to become a Friday chore. It can become somebody else's job." (finding 1).
- "This January, the tin could leave the house before the last weekend does" (finding 1). The reader no longer has any mention of the coming January (see finding 7).

**Changed**

- **The steps.** They were general advice to the reader: "photograph each receipt, match the week's photographs to your bank lines every Friday, and note anything odd". They are now what Priya does: she "photographs each receipt when she gets it", and on Friday matches the photographs to her bank lines and notes anything odd. The steps are now attributed to Priya, and photographing now happens when each receipt arrives rather than as part of the Friday session (findings 1 and 2).
- **The survey groups** now report what respondents said, in the source's wording: "at least once a week" rather than "every week", and "receipts" rather than "everything" (finding 5).
- **The implied claim that the habit wins back the weekend.** The original implied it through "another way to get the weekend back". The current text implies it through "also": Priya's habit answers the lost weekend too (finding 1; unsupported, see finding 9).
- **The heading** "Ten minutes on a Friday" is word for word the same, but what it claims has moved. In the original, the body argued against it and gave "ten minutes" no support. Now it stands for Priya's session, "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea." So it now claims, through her, how long a weekly session takes.

**Added** (all for finding 1)

- Priya moved to a session every Friday in March 2026, quoted as "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea." (`material.md`, interview).
- As the support team notes, a photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable (`material.md`, support note).
- Priya's habit answers the tin's quieter cost, the fading receipts. This is an inference joining the two claims above.

Apart from the changes listed above, paragraph 2, the heading's wording and the other sentences of paragraphs 1 and 4 are unchanged.

## How the text meets the brief

Brief: `brief.md`. No other brief was named, so none was overridden. Every question is answered. Question 12 leaves nothing still to research ("Nothing is left to find out"). Where a rating changed, the rating before the edit comes first.

**1. What is the assignment?** Fulfilled. The piece covers keeping receipts through the tax year, as a letter-length general piece for the newsletter, in `en_GB`, under the working title. It is 285 words by a plain word count, heading included. That is just under 300, but within "roughly 300 to 450". No search phrase was wanted.

**2. Which brand is the sender?** Partly fulfilled → partly fulfilled. Before, recommending an accountant went beyond the brand's remit of habits and its own app. Now it speaks as Larkspur Ledger ("our users", "our support team"), plain and friendly, and within that remit. But "most of us" (finding 6) briefly makes the sender one of its readers.

**3. What does the sender want to convey with this text?** Not fulfilled → partly fulfilled. The text now leads to Priya's habit without stating the message outright: she photographs each receipt when she gets it and matches the photographs every Friday. That is where the scanner fits. The accountant figure (finding 8) still points the reader somewhere else.

**4. Who is the reader?** Partly fulfilled → partly fulfilled. The text meets the reader: the tin, the drawer or inbox, 31 January, receipts that can't be claimed. Nothing says why now, so the reader loses the reason to start this autumn (finding 7).

**5. What is the text's angle?** Not fulfilled → partly fulfilled. The text now sticks to the weekly habit. The accountant figure is left as a side track, and "what makes January short" rests on an unsupported "also" (findings 8 and 9).

**6. What is the hook?** Fulfilled. The last weekend of January and the two receipts faded to blank (paragraphs 1–2) set out what is at stake before the habit comes in.

**7. How should the text be structured?** Not fulfilled → partly fulfilled.
- The one-sentence summary is only partly carried out: the text walks through a Friday session but doesn't show that it makes the return short.
- The hook is resolved for the faded receipts ("a photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable"). For the lost weekend it is resolved only through "also".
- The ending ties back to the faded-receipt half of the hook, not to the brief's empty tin (findings 9 and 10).

**8. What should be left out?** Fulfilled. There is no tax advice, no claim about which expenses are allowable, no other app, no price and no paid plan.

**9. What should the reader have understood afterwards?** Not fulfilled → partly fulfilled. The reader learns two things. The Friday session, matching the week's photographs to bank lines, takes about ten minutes. And photographing each receipt when it arrives leaves a copy that stays readable. The text doesn't carry the idea that this makes the January return a short job, because the material doesn't show it (finding 9).

**10. What should the reader feel, think or do afterwards?** Not fulfilled → partly fulfilled. The reader is left with the steps and "About ten minutes", which supports the belief that a weekly session is short. The accountant figure pulls elsewhere (finding 8). The measure is not assessed.

**11. What makes the text RIV for the reader, and does the brief hold together?** Partly fulfilled → partly fulfilled.
- Relevant: the January return, but no October timing.
- Interesting: the hook.
- Valuable: the Friday steps and Priya's example, both now present.

The brief's own chain check is answered.

**12. What sources do you know of, and what do you need to find out?** Partly fulfilled → partly fulfilled. The text now uses all three sources: the survey with its caveat, the interview and the support note. It still contains "most of us" (finding 6) and the implication in "also" (finding 9), neither of which the material supports.

## What else changed

The review replaced the text's "therefore". Old paragraphs 3–6 made the case for handing the tin to an accountant. They are now Priya's Friday session, the survey and a closing paragraph on faded receipts, so the text went from six paragraphs to five. It also replaced an unnamed source with a named one and removed an invented detail. The heading's wording is unchanged, and the final proofread made no corrections.
